title: Jason Cohen on selling SmartBear, the freedom line, and the Joy/Skill/Need framework
summary: Jason Cohen reflects on selling SmartBear and co-founding WP Engine. He covers the Rich vs King choice, the freedom line, options short of selling, sharing equity with employees, and a Joy/Skill/Need framework for deciding which role a founder should hold.

principles.text: Don't treat selling as binary; list every option first: partial financing, handing the company to your team, recurring revenue, coaching.
principles.quote: I thought it was binary black or white I sell or I you know I'm miserable

principles.text: Judge a decision by the options considered, not by the outcome, because luck plays a part.
principles.quote: you can't judge the decision based on the outcome um you can't judge whether your poker decision was good based on the outcome because there's luck also

principles.text: Founders often hold their company back; stepping aside and vesting hungry operators in can grow it far more.
principles.quote: the company doubled the next year and it had been growing at like 5% per year

principles.text: Wealth isn't linear: past a freedom line, more money changes little. Gross up taxes and inflation honestly when finding your number.
principles.quote: there's some line Beyond which even adding another zero doesn't really change whether you're happy

principles.text: Expected value is useless for one-shot decisions like selling a company; use a sure-thing versus gamble thought experiment to find your own risk appetite.
principles.quote: the concept of the weighted average or the concept of expected value is useless

principles.text: Use Joy, Skill and Need to check your role. Any two without the third is a trap; the goal is work that is all three.
principles.quote: if you have two of the three it's a trap because you feel good you feel like it's good and it's bad
